faq.a: Defective BLM helicase causes genomic instability, leading to accumulation of mutations and chromosomal rearrangements that drive malignancy.
faq.q: Why is cancer risk so high in Bloom syndrome?

faq.a: With strict sun protection, infection prevention and early cancer detection, many achieve adulthood, but lifespan is reduced compared with the general population.
faq.q: Can patients live a normal life with Bloom syndrome?

faq.a: No; treatment is supportive and preventive. Gene therapy is experimental and not available in low‑resource settings.

exam: What bedside findings would make you suspect Bloom syndrome in a 10‑year‑old with short stature? — Look for facial dysmorphism, photosensitive rash, and a history of recurrent infections; note proportionate dwarfism.
How would you confirm the diagnosis when chromosome breakage testing is unavailable? — Arrange targeted BLM gene sequencing on a dried blood spot sent to a reference lab.

A patient with known Bloom syndrome presents with a new abdominal mass. What is your next step? — Prioritise urgent imaging (ultrasound or CT) and refer for oncologic assessment; do not delay for routine labs.
Why is broad‑spectrum sunscreen essential in Bloom syndrome, and what SPF is recommended? — UV‑induced DNA damage triggers skin cancers; use SPF 50+ and reapply every 2 hours.

How does the cancer surveillance schedule for Bloom syndrome differ from the general population? — Begin colonoscopy at age 25, breast MRI at 30, and annual skin exams, earlier and more frequent than standard guidelines.

What distinguishes Bloom syndrome from Fanconi anaemia on cytogenetic testing? — Bloom shows markedly increased sister‑chromatid exchanges; Fanconi anaemia shows chromosome breakage with diepoxybutane or mitomycin C challenge.

In a low‑resource hospital lacking genetic testing, which clinical clues most strongly support Bloom syndrome? — Severe photosensitivity, proportionate short stature, characteristic facial features, and early‑onset malignancy in a consanguineous family.

Which medications should be avoided in Bloom syndrome patients and why? — Avoid DNA‑damaging agents (e.g., alkylating chemotherapy) unless treating a confirmed cancer, because baseline repair defect increases toxicity.
ai.title: Bloom Syndrome
ai.subject: Medicine
ai.summary: Bloom syndrome is an autosomal recessive DNA‑repair disorder causing short stature, photosensitivity and a markedly increased cancer risk. Diagnosis relies on clinical features and cytogenetic testing for sister‑chromatid exchanges.

b: Autosomal recessive inheritance
Characteristic facial features: narrow nose, long philtrum, prominent ears
Short stature and proportionate dwarfism
sections.p: Bloom syndrome is a rare genomic instability disorder caused by pathogenic variants in the BLM gene (RECQL3). The hallmark is a high frequency of spontaneous sister‑chromatid exchanges on chromosome analysis.

t.b: Confirms diagnosis; >10 exchanges per cell is diagnostic
Identifies pathogenic variants when cytogenetics unavailable
Detects anemia, immunodeficiency or organ dysfunction that may accompany the syndrome

b: Mild: normal lifespan, few infections, no cancer by age 30
Moderate: recurrent infections, early‑onset malignancy (<40 y)
Severe: multiple cancers, organ failure, death before 50 y
sections.p: There is no formal staging system; clinical severity is judged by growth impairment, frequency of malignancy, and presence of organ dysfunction.

b: Consanguineous families – most common in Ashkenazi Jewish and some East Asian populations
Rare sporadic mutations
sections.p: Pathogenic biallelic variants in the BLM gene impair helicase activity, leading to defective DNA repair and chromosomal instability.

b: Sun‑exposed erythema that heals with telangiectasia
Frequent otitis media, sinusitis, or pneumonia
Solid tumours (e.g., colorectal, breast, gastric) and haematologic malignancies
sections.p: Patients present in early childhood with proportionate short stature, photosensitive rash, and characteristic facial dysmorphism. Recurrent respiratory infections and early‑onset cancers are common later.
In low‑resource settings, focus on clinical clues and basic labs; refer for cytogenetic testing when possible.

t.b: Confirms photosensitivity pattern; guides sun‑avoidance advice
Detects cytopenias that may signal marrow involvement or infection
Screens for organomegaly or early tumours when CT unavailable

t.a: If chromosome breakage test unavailable, send dried blood spot for BLM sequencing to regional reference lab

b: Acute leukaemia presentation
Advanced solid tumour with obstruction
Severe immunodeficiency leading to sepsis
sections.p: Rapidly enlarging mass, unexplained weight loss, persistent fever, or new neurological deficits demand urgent evaluation for malignancy.

b: Strict photoprotection: broad‑spectrum sunscreen, protective clothing, avoid midday sun
Vaccinations (including pneumococcal and influenza) to reduce infection risk
Regular cancer surveillance: annual skin exam, colonoscopy from age 25, breast MRI for females from age 30
Prompt treatment of infections with appropriate antibiotics; avoid immunosuppressive drugs unless clearly indicated
sections.p: No curative therapy; management is preventive, supportive and cancer‑focused.

b: 6‑monthly clinical review with dermatologist and oncologist
Annual full blood count and liver/kidney function tests
Genetic counselling for siblings and future pregnancies
sections.p: Lifelong multidisciplinary follow‑up is essential. Counsel families about carrier testing and prenatal diagnosis.

b: Xeroderma pigmentosum – severe UV‑induced skin cancers, no sister‑chromatid exchanges
Fanconi anaemia – bone‑marrow failure, radial ray defects, different chromosomal breakage pattern
sections.p: Conditions sharing photosensitivity and short stature may be mistaken for Bloom syndrome.

b: Sister‑chromatid exchange count can be normal in early childhood; repeat testing if suspicion remains
Skin photosensitivity may be mild in tropical climates, leading to under‑recognition
sections.p: Normal routine blood counts do not exclude underlying DNA repair defect; a lack of overt cytopenia may give false reassurance.

whenToSeekHelp: Rapidly growing lump or new mass
